• Maximum length: up to 4.5 cm
  • Temperature: 22–28 °C
  • Very easy to keep, suitable for beginners

Its native habitat was unknown until 1980, although the species was described as early as 1937. The first description was based on aquarium fish imports whose origin was unknown and only vaguely stated as "probably Amazonas". Although breeding the fish is not easy (randomly matched pairs often do not spawn, the females have to be brought to spawn at regular intervals so that the spawn remains fertile, etc.), wild catches were hardly ever made and it was not until 1980 that Gery discovered that the home of the lemon tetra is in the lower Amazon basin, more precisely in the middle and lower Tapajós between Itaituba and Jacare Acanga, as well as in streams that flow into the Rio Curua do Sol. Other authors also mention the Xingu and the Tocantins.

Wild catches of H. pulchripinnis from the Rio Cuiaba in the state of Mato Grosso (Brazil) have recently been received. This is an extremely rare event.
In nature, the water is almost always cloudy due to clay or other suspended particles.
Keeping all lemon tetras is very easy and even beginners can manage it. The animals are kept in groups in well-structured aquaria, where each fish soon occupies a tiny territory.
The temperature can be between 22 and 28 °C. The water should (but does not have to) be soft and slightly acidic, then the colors are at their best.
They will eat any common fish food.

Freshly caught animals are crystal red, but in the aquarium they usually discolor. This phenomenon is known from many fish species. The cause is most probably clean aquarium water; in nature the water is almost always cloudy. Coloration is controlled by hormones whose production is triggered by stimuli perceived by the eye (light, shade, water turbidity, color of the substrate, etc.). This explains why most fish in bright, sparsely furnished aquariums are very pale, but not why they sometimes show bright colors after a certain period.

"Muzel Red Cherry" tetras are imports from Brazil, presumably bred there. They are predominantly bright red, but some have a yellow body color and look very similar to lemon tetras. In yellow Muzel tetras the humeral spot is strongly pronounced, while it is only faintly visible in red ones. All fins of both Muzel colors are bright red, which distinguishes them from "true" lemon tetras, which at best have faintly orange dorsal and anal fins. The caudal fin of "true" lemon tetras is always transparent and colorless. "Bolivia Orange" lemon tetras share this characteristic.

There is a whole circle of forms around H. pulchripinnis: 1. the "classic" H. pulchripinnis, in aquaria since 1937 (colorless caudal fin, usually also dorsal and anal fins, anal fin with yellow and black line on the leading edge, dorsal fin also with black on the leading edge); 2. the pulchripinnis "Tapajós", which lacks the black line at the beginning of the anal and dorsal fin and is apparently not represented in the hobby or not distinguished from the normal lemon tetra; 3. the "Bolivia Orange", in the hobby since around 1980 (colorless caudal fin, dorsal and anal fins bright red, black line on the anal fin missing); 4. the "Muzel Cherry Red", in which all fins and body are bright red, black line on the anal fin missing, in the hobby since about 2021; 5. the "Muzel Yellow", like the "Muzel Cherry Red" but with a yellow-orange body.
